transcription_uncertainty: The summaries are based on live transcriptions (Reachy Mini). Automatic speech recognition is uncertain in places (names and technical terms are often distorted). Reachy timestamps typically run about one hour earlier than the official programme times (presumably UTC rather than CET). No verbatim quotations are presented as confirmed.
takeaways: AI has an effect in planning, construction and operations primarily when processes, data and organisation are changed along with it – not when new tools are simply dropped into old workflows.
Agents can prepare routine work (reports, bills of quantities drafts, notes, appointments); approval, assessment and responsibility remain with the specialists.
Without structured, end-to-end data (components, zones, times, sensor data, ERP), orchestration and predictive operations remain ineffective – “Garbage in, Garbage out”.
In early-stage planning, AI is particularly useful because the data is poor while the leverage of decisions is high; precision and traceability must be managed deliberately.

On the construction site and in existing buildings, automation, measurement quality and transparency often come first (drilling from the model, fan condition, room and energy data, LED and refurbishment measures) – AI comes as the next step.
Cybersecurity and redundancy belong in the planning of building automation, not as an afterthought (example: secure controllers according to IEC 62443).
Leadership and culture also decide: spaces to experiment, skills development, and the question of what saved time is used for.
Participants were told that transcripts and a way to ask questions would be made available in the days after the event.

eroeffnung.abstract: The mayor of Kernen, Benedikt Paulowitsch, welcomes the guests together with host Heino Wolkenhauer, Geschäftsführer of Wilhelm Schetter GmbH Haustechnik. (Flyer: welcomes the guests with Heino Wolkenhauer and Michael Aechtler.)
summary_bullets: Heino Wolkenhauer opened the Praxisforum and reported that the host company has been using AI for about a year – with efficiency gains and a shift from initial scepticism to enthusiasm.
The aim of the day was to share experience and concrete applications, to put questions to the speakers, and to exchange views at the stands.
According to the welcome, more than 400 participants from planning, industry, construction, academia and the media were present.
Mayor Benedikt Paulowitsch praised the organisers’ courage, called AI an opportunity for Germany, and presented Kernen as a pioneer municipality in public administration.
What matters for the use of AI is a change in organisation, culture and attitude – not merely the purchase of tools.

impuls-1-liebl.abstract: AI is moving from a tool to a co-worker: agents take on tasks and responsibility – often faster than organisations can adapt. Introducing tools alone does little: employees work up to 70% faster, yet lead time barely falls because the work waits at old interfaces. Only an end-to-end redesign of processes makes silos disappear. Using practical examples, the talk sets out six maturity stages through to a self-optimising organisation – and what that means for leadership.
summary_bullets: Liebl placed the development in context: from specialised machine-learning applications, through generative AI (summarising, researching, producing text and images), to agents that can operate tools, plan, and hand sub-tasks to sub-agents.
Tools alone often change throughput very little: in a simulation example shown in the talk, lead time fell noticeably only when processes were recut – not merely when individual steps became faster.
In the operating model sketched, people remain the instance that assesses, queries and approves results, while AI takes over large parts of the execution.

As the next generation of value creation he described the interplay of manager agents (short- and long-term memory, planning, tools) with freely configurable agent structures – and a corresponding transformation and leadership effort.
Questions of safety and control (agent setups that cannot be fully controlled, research examples of communication between systems) were raised as an open leadership task.

impuls-2-aechtler.abstract: Everyone talks about AI, yet little has changed so far in the everyday work of planning offices, construction sites and building operations. Michael Aechtler shows live how an AI agent really works alongside people today: it listens in meetings, sorts notes, drafts proposals and prepares appointments. Using his own company, which is to a large extent run with AI agents, it becomes clear which data and preconditions are needed, where time and cost are saved, and where the limits lie. There are also concrete first steps with which companies can move from trying things out to taking action and take their employees with them.
summary_bullets: Aechtler picked up the finding that there is much talk about AI, yet everyday work in planning, construction and operations often still changes little – and demonstrated live how an agent works on concrete office tasks.

The live demo included, among other things, an agent interface (documented in event photos as “HALLO MICHAEL”); the talk showed typical activities such as listening in meetings, sorting notes, and preparing proposals and appointments.
The example was his own company, which according to the speaker is to a large extent run with AI agents; the necessary data and preconditions were as visible as the limits of automation.
The keynote aimed at concrete first steps: moving from trying things out to taking action and taking employees along, rather than stopping at tool demos.

impuls-3-huber.abstract: Company performance does not come from AI alone, but from its successful integration into a company’s value creation. The winners in the AI era will not be the companies with the most tools, but the companies that connect technology, data, people and processes into a high-performing value-creation system.
summary_bullets: Huber introduced herself as responsible for Digital Strategy & Culture at Drees & Sommer and framed the keynote around the question of how data actually becomes higher company performance.
Performance does not come from the greatest number of AI tools, but from connecting technology, data, people and processes into a value-creation system.
On slides about digital transformation (also documented in photographs) she showed that strategy, collaboration and culture are just as decisive as the technical layer.
The talk ended with an outlook on deep-seated change (“Alles wird anders”) and the call to think about performance across the whole organisation, not only through individual pilot projects.

pause-foren.abstract: The keynotes have shown which organisational and technical preconditions are necessary. The specialist forums now turn to concrete applications, data structures, solutions and experience from planning, execution and operations. (Flyer: Pause & Networking – transition to the specialist forums until 18:10.)
summary_bullets: After the three keynotes the first part of the programme was closed and a break was announced; from 15:30 guests were to spread out across the specialist forums and the trade exhibition.
It was promised that the content would be transcribed and that, within the following one to three days, a link to a platform would be sent through which questions could still be asked afterwards.

f1-bengel.abstract: Planning and construction processes are becoming more complex, the volume of available information is growing, and at the same time decisions have to be taken ever faster. The talk shows how digital methods can shorten the path from information to decision. This is not only about BIM or AI. Automation, structured data and digital applications can also reduce routine work, make changes visible early and make relevant information available more quickly. That leaves more time for the actual professional assessment and decision.
summary_bullets: Bengel (in the transcript “Patricia Bengel”) introduced herself with a focus on strategy and development at ATP and framed the talk as the path from information to decision.
Growing data volumes and rising time pressure in planning and construction make it necessary to reduce routine work so that professional assessment remains.
Besides BIM and AI she named automation and structured data as means of making changes visible earlier and relevant information available more quickly.
AI was described as an amplifier that needs a foundation of data that is as clean and consistent as possible – not as a substitute for the professional decision.

f1-wuerth.abstract: Orchestrating AI systems that independently steer procurement and delivery on the construction site rarely fail because of the control logic – but because of missing, end-to-end data supply. Component data, project zones and ERP processes today usually run in separate systems. Using fastening technology as an example, the talk shows how a consistent link between component, zone and SAP data creates the foundation on which a higher-level AI can in future coordinate procurement and delivery independently. The focus is therefore not the AI itself, but the data basis without which any orchestration remains ineffective.
summary_bullets: In the transcript Matthäus Grzondziel (ASR: “Matthias”) introduces himself for Würth; Sven Assmann is a co-speaker according to the programme, but was not found by name in the transcript.
Central thesis: orchestration of procurement and delivery rarely fails because of the control logic, but because of missing, end-to-end data supply.
Components need a clear spatial assignment (project zones, not just “a room”) and a link to the schedule, so that place and time become reliable information.
Logistical pacing can follow from this: the system derives from construction progress when something is needed and must be provided.
Without structured data, “Garbage in, Garbage out” applies: unstructured or incorrect inputs lead an AI at high speed into wrong decisions.

f1-tsagkalidi.abstract_note: On the event website and in the flyer, only the title is given, no abstract.
summary_bullets: For this time window there is a transcript passage that was matched only via the programme clock (Reachy time plus about one hour); name and company are not clearly stated in this section.
A substantively reliable, speaker-specific summary is therefore not possible without speculation.

f1-jaeger.abstract: Industry is demanding ever more detailed BIM models, while planning budgets are under pressure. Not infrequently, the effort of modelling individual plant components exceeds the effort of installing them later. At the same time, planning fees often lie below the material mark-ups of the trades involved. The result: without new tools, digital planning is barely still viable economically. Using concrete practical examples from technical building services, the talk shows how artificial intelligence evaluates drawings and schematics, determines quantities automatically, and takes component and area data directly into calculations.
f1-jaeger.company_note: Flyer: EFG Engineering Facility Group Ingenieurgesellschaft mbH
summary_bullets: The contribution sits in the time window of Jäger’s programme slot; the name “Jäger” appears in the transcript, though not as a clear self-introduction – the assignment is probable, not necessarily certain.

The core theme according to the announcement and matching transcript passages: modelling effort in TGA planning threatens to outweigh the benefit when BIM models become ever more detailed and budgets tighter.
AI can evaluate drawings and schematics, determine quantities, and take component and area data into calculations – and so make digital planning economically viable again.
Professional responsibility and checking remain with the engineers.

f1-duftschmid.abstract: What happens when a classical engineering office is organised in a hybrid way – people and AI agents working together with a division of labour? Using the example of a Munich planning office with 20 employees, this talk shows how that works in practice: five AI agents take on defined tasks in day-to-day work – from preparing explanatory reports and researching standards to personal assistance. A report that used to take 2–3 hours is today prepared in 10 minutes – checking and approval remain with the engineer. The talk sets out the necessary preconditions (data, processes, responsibilities) and the concrete benefit for planners, clients and operators.
summary_bullets: For the 16:50 time window there is a transcript passage that was matched only via the clock; the name Duftschmid is not clearly stated in this section.

According to the published talk announcement (not as evidence from a recording), the subject is five agents in a hybrid-organised office and reports that are prepared but checked and approved by the engineer.
A speaker-specific summary from the transcript of this window alone would be speculative and is therefore omitted.

f1-ocklenburg.abstract: In work stages 6 and 7 – preparing and assisting with the tender – it is decided how quickly and economically a project is put out to tender. Using a tender as an example, the talk shows how AI produces a structured, GAEB-exportable draft bill of quantities from the plan and the building description – and where its limits lie. The often overlooked other side: every benefit of AI arises from data. Does the platform become a black box – or do you keep control? The talk shows what AI reliably takes on, where people retain responsibility, and how planners and clients keep their bidder and price data – transparent and exportable at any time.
summary_bullets: In the transcript the company Cosuno is named as a tendering and awarding platform for work stages 6 and 7; the person’s name is not clear, but the match to the programme slot is probable.
AI can prepare a structured, GAEB-exportable draft bill of quantities from the plan and the building description, but reaches professional limits that people must take responsibility for.
Every benefit arises from data: what matters is that the platform does not become a black box and that bidder and price data remain with planners and clients – transparent and exportable.

f1-aghasi.abstract: How does one take energy and building-services decisions early, quickly and reliably, before they become expensive? AI-supported energy simulation on the basis of BIM/IFC speeds up TGA planning, supports compliance with national energy rules, and makes value engineering data-based. Example: for a general contractor we assessed a new building of around 200,000 m² GFA in the tender. After four weeks the energy class was available, instead of conventionally more than four months. Clients compare variants while changes are still cheap, planners save variant calculations, bidders an expensive certification. Operators reduce operating costs and have an ESG/EPBD basis.
summary_bullets: The first name “Nomi” appears in the transcript shortly before this time window; the assignment to Nomi Aghasi / OPTIMUSE is therefore probable.
The topic is the early, reliable assessment of energy and TGA variants, before changes become expensive – by simulation on the basis of building data (BIM/IFC).
As a practical benchmark the announcement (and matching transcript passages on acceleration) cited an energy class in weeks rather than months, for example on a large new building.
Benefit arises for clients (comparing variants), planners (fewer manual variant calculations) and operators (operating costs, ESG basis).

f1-petraus.abstract: In the early planning phase, the decisions with the greatest leverage fall at the poorest data situation a project will ever have. Established tools demand completeness where nothing is yet complete. AI proves more robust; it can work with little, unstructured data, but brings other problems: precision, reproducibility, traceability. The talk sorts applications, from survey of the existing building to the formation of variants, by how quickly an error becomes visible. Used properly, more checked variants arise more quickly, and with them better-justified decisions. The energy-system planning of an industrial site serves as a stress test.
summary_bullets: In the transcript the TMM Group is named in this time window; the assignment to Bernd Petraus is probable.
Early planning decisions have the greatest leverage but the poorest data; classical tools often presuppose completeness that does not yet exist.
AI can work with little, unstructured data, but raises questions of precision, reproducibility and traceability.

Applications from survey of the existing building through to the formation of variants were sorted by how quickly an error becomes visible – with the energy-system planning of an industrial site as a stress test.

f2-muehlenbruch.abstract: From the BIM model to the automated construction site: digital planning creates the foundation for prefabrication, automated processes and the use of robotics in construction. Concrete practical examples from BIM-supported fastening planning, digital logistics and the use of the Jaibot drilling robot show how end-to-end data flows connect planning and execution. The talk shows how construction companies can raise productivity, respond to the shortage of skilled labour, and achieve more quality, transparency and certainty of schedule and cost.
summary_bullets: After a brief introduction (“Firma Hildi”), “Axel Mbruch” introduces himself as technical lead for engineering and robotics – the assignment to Axel Mühlenbruch, Hilti, is probable.

The talk was to show the path from the digital model (TGA model on the slide) to the automated construction site, specifically to the drilling robot, which does not drill “by itself” but needs position and drilling points.
A typical BIM/TGA model alone is not enough for drilling: the information is too rudimentary; an end-to-end chain is needed from planning through to the machine on site.
Mühlenbruch stressed that there is often still less AI here than in the preceding keynotes, but instead concrete automation that can be used in practice.

f2-mueller.abstract: How does a fan become an intelligent system component? The talk shows how operating data, AI and digital services enable the step from reactive to predictive maintenance. Using vibration and bearing monitoring as an example, it becomes clear how AI assesses conditions and, beyond that, can support the entire service chain from diagnosis and assistance through to continuous optimisation.
summary_bullets: The contribution is announced in the transcript as a talk by “Zell Abig” / “Zel Abig”, expressly as a fan manufacturer for building services – the assignment to ZIEHL-ABEGG is probable; the personal name André Müller does not appear.
The topic is recognising conditions on the fan and avoiding failures (predictive maintenance, typically via vibration and bearing signals).
Because the speaker’s name is missing, the statements are deliberately limited to the company and the topic.

f2-belimo.abstract: Using a meeting room in daily use as an example, the talk shows how high-quality data leads to better decisions in building operations. Precise room sensors record temperature, CO₂ and humidity reliably, including under real installation conditions. The Belimo Energy Valve measures the power actually supplied and optimises operation directly via the ΔT-Manager. In the MID-certified version, the energy values can also serve as a basis for possible billing. When room, plant and energy data are brought together, transparency, efficiency and a robust basis for AI-supported analyses and further optimisations are created.
summary_bullets: One person introduces themselves as being from Belimo (“Wir machen die orangenen Antriebe”); which of the two programme names (Philipp Becker, Alexander Saumer) is speaking is unclear from the speech recognition.
According to the announcement and matching transcript passages, high-quality room and energy data come at the start of good operating decisions (temperature, CO₂, humidity).
On the product side, the Energy Valve or the measurement of the power actually supplied, and the use of certified energy data as a basis for analyses and possible billing, were discussed.
Combined room, plant and energy data are intended to create transparency, efficiency and a basis for later AI analyses.

f2-voelkerling.abstract: How can we use AI profitably in processes and products? That is a question every company faces today. In the ventilation sector too we use AI to optimise internal processes and to advance projects on the use of AI in our products. Where do we stand in this development today? What are the preconditions for the successful use of AI? At TROX, AI is already used in several areas: in production, AI helps to detect anomalies early; in sales, orders are captured automatically. Internal chatbots support the search for information; in research, the use of machine learning for fault detection in air-handling units is being trialled.
summary_bullets: Völkerling introduces herself by name and places herself in the AI team of IT at TROX (for about five years) – the assignment is certain.
The talk offered practical experience of using AI in ventilation technology, not merely a promise for the future.

In the transcript and in the advance description, applications appear in production (anomaly detection), sales (for example automatic order capture) and internal assistants, as well as machine learning for fault detection on air-handling units.

f2-rauh.abstract: The decarbonisation of existing buildings confronts owners with the challenge of meeting climate targets, economic viability and security of supply at the same time. Using the modular refurbishment of a care home as an example, it is shown how a step-by-step transformation can succeed during ongoing operation. At the same time it is shown how the preconditions for energy-flexible operation in the future can already be created today, in order to be prepared for dynamic energy markets, grid requirements and new business models.
f2-rauh.company_note: Event website: Bosch Energy and Building Solutions GmbH. Flyer: Buderus. Participant dossier: Bosch Energy and Building Solutions / Buderus.
summary_bullets: Thematically the section clearly matches the programme title on energy flexibility through modular refurbishment of a care home; the person speaking introduces themselves in the transcript as “Christian” from “Firma Bosch” – not as Johannes Rauh. The person’s identity is therefore unclear and should be checked.

The contribution describes the pressure of electrification (heat pumps, process heat, flexible tariffs, storage, building connection) on existing buildings such as businesses and care or health facilities.
Modular refurbishment is intended to connect energy efficiency, security of supply and flexibility, without underestimating the complexity of the energy transition.

f2-helbig.abstract: How does a manufacturing company identify savings potential and assess investments on a sound basis? Brugger Magnetsysteme brings energy data from production, building services and photovoltaics together centrally in the Mondas data platform. The measured data show what measures really deliver: the LED conversion, for example, reduced electricity consumption by around 50%. At the same time, real load profiles form the basis for addressing PV self-consumption, load peaks and battery storage in a targeted way. The talk shows how energy data become decisions and how energy costs can in future be attributed to individual machines and products.
summary_bullets: In the transcript, “Monondas”, the conversation with Geschäftsführer Thomas Brugger and the case of a manufacturer of magnet systems appear; the name Miriam Helbig is missing. It is mentioned that they are appearing “zu dritt” (as a group of three). The slot assignment is probable, the exact speaker role unclear.
The starting point at the customer was transparency over machine consumption, not “AI for AI’s sake” first.

Energy data from production, building services and photovoltaics are brought together on a data platform; a documented example is the LED conversion with a marked reduction in electricity consumption (in the announcement: around 50%).
The aim is to derive decisions from measured data and, looking ahead, to attribute energy costs to machines and products.

f2-ferstl.abstract: In modern production and clean-room plants, cybersecurity is increasingly becoming a fundamental requirement for building automation. Using the example of a newly built high-tech production plant in Berlin, the talk shows how cybersecurity, high availability and high-performance automation can be combined. The Saia PCD QronoX controller is used, with Security Level 3 according to IEC 62443 and a redundant control architecture. The connection via BACnet enables integration into the building automation. The practical case shows how cybersecurity can already be implemented consistently down to the controller level when a new building is planned.
summary_bullets: Ferstl introduces himself by name as Vertriebsleiter Süd; the company sounds in the transcript like “S Birges Co” (Saia Burgess Controls / SBC) – the assignment is certain.
The topic is secure and redundant automation (in the transcript “Korrugsteuerung”) with cybersecurity according to IEC 62443, Security Level 3.
High availability and security are to be thought together, not as a later add-on; the practical case is aimed at a high-tech production environment.
The controller should be integrable into the building automation; cybersecurity begins already in planning, not only in operation.

f2-pfau.abstract: How can AI make building operations more predictive without taking people out of responsibility? Using the practical example of predictive and prescriptive maintenance, the talk shows how operating data from building automation and HVAC are used to detect deviations early, narrow down causes and prioritise measures. Preconditions are connected systems, structured and contextualised data, and clear goals and rights of intervention. AI supports analysis and workflows; people set guardrails and validate decisions. In this way, effort and operational risks can be reduced and availability, energy efficiency and user comfort improved.
summary_bullets: The speaker introduces himself as “Simon V” of Siemens AG – the assignment to Simon Pfau is probable.
Many so-called smart buildings remain a patchwork of individual solutions and dashboards; the next step is to link data across them.
The vision (already partly reality) is the human-centric, autonomous building: AI helps to detect deviations early and propose measures; people set guardrails and remain responsible.

As preconditions he named connectivity, a data strategy already in planning (“Smart Ready”) and clear use cases in operation; in average figures he spoke of noticeable energy-cost reductions when flexible generators and consumers work together.

abschluss.abstract: From impulse to implementation: the next steps. Michael Aechtler and Heino Wolkenhauer.
